bib.title: Reinforcement Learning: A Comprehensive Overview, Chapter 2: Value-based RL

question: How are value functions defined and learned, from dynamic programming with a known model through Monte Carlo, TD, SARSA and Q-learning to deep Q-learning and its extensions?
contributions: Survey of value-based RL: Bellman equations, DP (VI, PI, RTDP), MC, TD(lambda), eligibility traces, SARSA, Q-learning, DQN and its extensions (double, dueling, noisy, multi-step, Rainbow, BBF), hindsight relabeling

results.claim: Rainbow combines 6 improvements to vanilla DQN and gave SOTA on Atari-200M in 2018.
results.quote: The Rainbow method of [Hes+18] combined 6 improvements to the vanilla DQN method, as listed below.

results.claim: Rainbow's n-step component uses n = 3.
results.quote: Use n-step returns (with n = 3), as in Section 2.5.4.4.

results.claim: Each Rainbow component gives diminishing returns (read from Fig 2.9, median human-normalised score over 57 Atari games).
results.quote: Each improvement gives diminishing returns, as can be see in Figure 2.9.

results.claim: BBF (Bigger, Better, Faster) is SOTA on the 100k sample-efficient Atari benchmark as of 2024.
results.quote: At the time of writing this document (2024), the SOTA on the 100k sample-efficient Atari benchmark [Kai+19]

results.claim: BBF anneals the n-step return from n = 10 to n = 3 to reduce bias over time.
results.quote: gradually decrease (anneal) the n-step return from n = 10 to n = 3, to reduce the bias over time.

results.claim: BBF raises the discount factor from 0.97 to 0.997 during training.
results.quote: Gradually increase the discount factor from γ = 0.97 to γ = 0.997, to encourage longer term planning

results.claim: BBF ranks its tricks; the larger residual Impala-style CNN is the most important, then higher update-to-data ratio, then periodic soft resets.
results.quote: It uses the following tricks, in order of decreasing importance:

results.claim: BBF drops noisy nets because they do not help and need multiple network copies.
results.quote: Drop noisy nets (which requires multiple network copies and thus slows down training due to increased memory use), since it does not help.

results.claim: Agent57 reached superhuman performance on all 57 Atari games but needed 80 billion frames; MEME reduced this to the standard 200M frames.
results.source: Badia et al. 2020; Kapturowski et al. 2022
results.quote: However, it required 80 billion frames (environment steps)! This was subsequently reduced to the “standard” 200M frames in the MEME method of [Kap+22].

results.claim: Atari-100k contains only 26 of the 46 ALE games, those solvable by model-free deep RL in 2019.
results.quote: The Atari-100k benchmark only includes 26 out of 46 games of the ALE

results.claim: Prioritised replay sets priority p_i = (delta_i + eps)^alpha; alpha = 0 is uniform sampling.
results.quote: α ≥0 determines the degree of prioritization, with α = 0 corresponding to no prioritization (uniform sampling).

results.claim: Baird's counterexample has 7 states, 2 actions, gamma 0.99, w in R^8; TD(0) with behaviour probabilities 6/7 dashed and 1/7 solid diverges to infinity though the true value is 0.
results.setup: Baird counterexample, linear V_w, off-policy TD(0), gamma = 0.99
results.quote: If we apply TD(0) on this trajectory, the parameters diverge to ∞(Figure 2.6b), even though the problem appears simple.

results.claim: The deadly triad is function approximation plus bootstrapping plus off-policy learning.
results.quote: This combination is known as the deadly triad

results.claim: Target-network EMA uses forgetting factor rho of about 0.999.
results.setup: DQN-style target network by EMA of weights
results.quote: where the forgetting factor ρ ≈0.999 ensures that Qw slowly catches up with Qw.

results.claim: Bounded final-layer weights, wide penultimate layer and bounded-norm critic input (LayerNorm/RMSNorm) are sufficient for off-policy nonlinear TD to converge.
results.quote: [Gal+24] proved that nonlinear TD learning can be made to converge, even in the off-policy setting, if three simple conditions on the critic (Q network) are satisfied

results.claim: Maximization-bias example: action B draws rewards from N(-0.1, 1.0), expected return -0.1, yet Q-learning may prefer the left action; double Q-learning fixes it (eps = 0.1, 10,000 runs).
results.setup: Fig 2.8 toy MDP, eps-greedy eps = 0.1, averaged over 10,000 runs
results.quote: with rewards drawn from N(−0.1, 1.0). Thus the expected return for any trajectory starting with the left action is −0.1, making it suboptimal.

results.claim: REDQ uses N > 2 Q-networks, samples M <= N and takes the min; N = M = 2 resembles clipped double Q; it relies on UTD G >> 1.
results.quote: Furthermore, at each step, it draws a random sample of M ≤N networks, and takes the minimum over them when computing the target value.

results.claim: Dueling DQN: Q = V + A - mean A (the paper says the max in the identifiability constraint is replaced by an average, which works better empirically).
results.quote: In practice, the max is replaced by an average, which seems to work better empirically.

results.claim: Beyond the Rainbow (2024) adds a larger Impala CNN, IQN in place of C51, Munchausen RL and 64 parallel workers with 1 env step each per minibatch update.
results.quote: Collect 1 environment step from 64 parallel workers for each minibatch update

results.claim: Value iteration is a gamma-contraction: max error shrinks by factor gamma each iteration.
results.quote: every iteration will reduce the maximum value function error by a constant factor.

results.claim: 1d grid world with gamma = 0.9 gives Q* values 1.0, 0.9, 0.81, 0.73 along the path (Fig 2.1d).
results.quote: This reflects a preference for near-term rewards, while also taking future reward into account.

results.claim: Q-learning worked example uses gamma = 0.9, step size eta = 1, Q initialised to zero, eps-greedy.
results.quote: We initialize Q(s, a) = 0 for all entries, and use a step size of η = 1.

limits: No experiments of its own; all empirical statements (Rainbow, BBF, Agent57) are reported from other work.
Distributional RL (C51, QR-DQN, IQN) is only named here and deferred to Section 7.3, not explained.
Rainbow component diminishing-returns claim rests on Fig 2.9 only; no ablation numbers are printed in the text.
SOTA statements are as of 2024 and have dated.
Chapter says the Q(lambda) off-policy case is more complicated and gives no algorithm.
practices: Use a frozen target network (periodic copy or EMA with rho about 0.999) with a stop-gradient to stabilise DQN targets (2.5.2.6).
Use experience replay to improve data efficiency and decorrelate samples; it requires an off-policy method (2.5.2.3).
Use double DQN: select actions with the online net and evaluate with the target net to reduce maximisation bias (2.5.3.2).
Use LayerNorm or RMSNorm on critic features and bound final-layer weights to keep off-policy TD stable (2.5.2.9).
Include (1 - done(s')) in the Q-learning target; omitted from equations but required in code (2.5.1, Eq 2.33).
Use dueling heads with advantage mean-subtraction (2.5.4.2).
For multi-step DQN, restrict replay sampling to recent data to stay approximately on-policy (2.5.4.4).
Raise update-to-data ratio with periodic soft resets and anneal n-step and gamma for sample efficiency (BBF, 2.5.4.7).
Use hindsight relabeling with any off-policy method for goal-conditioned RL when reward is Markovian (2.5.5).

code.snippet: Q(s, a) ←Q(s, a) + η [ r + γ max_a′ Q(s′, a′) −Q(s, a) ]
Q(s, a) ←Q(s, a) + η [ r + (1 −done(s′))γ max_a′ Q(s′, a′) −Q(s, a) ]
y(r, s′; w, w̄) = r + γ Q_w̄(s′, argmax_a′ Q_w(s′, a′))
Q_w(s, a) = V_w(s) + A_w(s, a) − max_a′ A_w(s, a′)
